paper_title: Comprehensive Named Entity Recognition on CORD-19 with Distant or Weak Supervision

questions.question: Did they experiment with the dataset?
expected_passages: In Figure FIGREF28, we show some examples of the annotation results in CORD-19-NER. We can see that our distantly- or weakly supervised methods achieve high quality recognizing the new entity types, requiring only several seed examples as the input. For example, we recognized “SARS-CoV-2" as the “CORONAVIRUS" type, “bat" and “pangolins" as the “WILDLIFE" type and “Van der Waals forces" as the “PHYSICAL_SCIENCE" type. This NER annotation results help downstream text mining tasks in discovering the origin and the physical nature of the virus. Our NER methods are domain-independent that can be applied to corpus in different domains. In addition, we show another example of NER annotation on New York Times with our system in Figure FIGREF29.

In Figure FIGREF30, we show the comparison of our annotation results with existing NER/BioNER systems. In Figure FIGREF30, we can see that only our method can identify “SARS-CoV-2" as a coronavirus. In Figure FIGREF30, we can see that our method can identify many more entities such as “pylogenetic" as a evolution term and “bat" as a wildlife. In Figure FIGREF30, we can also see that our method can identify many more entities such as “racism" as a social behavior. In summary, our distantly- and weakly-supervised NER methods are reliable for high-quality entity recognition without requiring human effort for training data annotation.

questions.question: What is the size of this dataset?
expected_passages: Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental step in text mining system development to facilitate the COVID-19 studies. There is critical need for NER methods that can quickly adapt to all the COVID-19 related new types without much human effort for training data annotation. We created this CORD-19-NER dataset with comprehensive named entity annotation on the CORD-19 corpus (2020-03-13). This dataset covers 75 fine-grained named entity types. CORD-19-NER is automatically generated by combining the annotation results from four sources. In the following sections, we introduce the details of CORD-19-NER dataset construction. We also show some NER annotation results in this dataset.

The corpus is generated from the 29,500 documents in the CORD-19 corpus (2020-03-13). We first merge all the meta-data (all_sources_metadata_2020-03-13.csv) with their corresponding full-text papers. Then we create a tokenized corpus (CORD-19-corpus.json) for further NER annotations.

questions.question: What four annotation sources are combined to build the dataset?
questions.ground_truth: A pre-trained Spacy NER model for 18 general entity types, a pre-trained SciSpacy NER model for 18 biomedical entity types, a knowledge-base-guided distantly-supervised NER model for 127 biomedical entity types, and a seed-guided weakly-supervised NER model for new COVID-19-specific entity types.
expected_passages: It is automatically generated by combining the annotation results from four sources: (1) pre-trained NER model on 18 general entity types from Spacy, (2) pre-trained NER model on 18 biomedical entity types from SciSpacy, (3) knowledge base (KB)-guided NER model on 127 biomedical entity types with our distantly-supervised NER method, and (4) seed-guided NER model on 8 new entity types (specifically related to the COVID-19 studies) with our weakly-supervised NER method.

questions.question: How many new COVID-19-specific entity types are added by the weakly-supervised method, and how many seed entities does each require?
questions.ground_truth: 9 new entity types, each requiring only about 10-20 human-input seed entities
expected_passages: Seed-guided NER on 9 new entity types (specifically related to the COVID-19 studies) with our weakly-supervised NER method. We only require several (10-20) human-input seed entities for each new type. Then we expand the seed entity sets with CatE and apply our distant NER method for the new entity type recognition.

expected_passages: Knowledge base (KB)-guided NER on 127 biomedical entity types with our distantly-supervised NER methods,. We do not require any human annotated training data for the NER model training. Instead, We rely on UMLS as the input KB for distant supervision.

questions.question: What is the CORD-19-NER dataset and what need does it address?
questions.ground_truth: It is a comprehensive named-entity-recognition dataset built automatically on the CORD-19 COVID-19 literature corpus. It addresses the critical need for NER methods that can quickly adapt to all the COVID-19-related new entity types without much human effort for training-data annotation.
expected_passages: Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental step in text mining system development to facilitate the COVID-19 studies. There is critical need for NER methods that can quickly adapt to all the COVID-19 related new types without much human effort for training data annotation.

questions.question: How do the four NER methods differ in the amount of human supervision they require?
questions.ground_truth: The Spacy and SciSpacy models are already pre-trained and need no new supervision. The KB-guided distantly-supervised method requires no human-annotated training data at all, relying instead on the UMLS knowledge base. The seed-guided weakly-supervised method requires only a handful (about 10-20) of human-input seed entities per new type, which are then expanded automatically with CatE.
expected_passages: Knowledge base (KB)-guided NER on 127 biomedical entity types with our distantly-supervised NER methods,. We do not require any human annotated training data for the NER model training. Instead, We rely on UMLS as the input KB for distant supervision.

Seed-guided NER on 9 new entity types (specifically related to the COVID-19 studies) with our weakly-supervised NER method. We only require several (10-20) human-input seed entities for each new type. Then we expand the seed entity sets with CatE and apply our distant NER method for the new entity type recognition.

questions.question: How are the annotations from the four sources merged into a single dataset?
questions.ground_truth: All entity types from the four sources are reorganized into one type hierarchy: SciSpacy types are aligned to UMLS, and some fine-grained UMLS types are merged into coarser ones based on corpus counts, yielding 75 fine-grained types. Each method then annotates the corpus, the results are merged into one file, and conflicts are resolved by giving priority to entity types from different methods according to their annotation quality.
expected_passages: We merged all the entity types from the four sources and reorganized them into one entity type hierarchy. Specifically, we align all the types from SciSpacy to UMLS. We also merge some fine-grained UMLS entity types to their more coarse-grained types based on the corpus count. Then we get a final entity type hierarchy with 75 fine-grained entity types used in our annotations.

After we get the NER annotation results with the four different methods, we merge the results into one file. The conflicts are resolved by giving priority to different entity types annotated by different methods according to their annotation quality.

questions.question: What do the authors claim about the domain-independence of their NER methods?
questions.ground_truth: They claim the distantly- and weakly-supervised NER methods are domain-independent and can be applied to corpora in different domains, not just COVID-19 literature - demonstrated by additionally running the system on New York Times text.
expected_passages: Our NER methods are domain-independent that can be applied to corpus in different domains. In addition, we show another example of NER annotation on New York Times with our system in Figure FIGREF29.

questions.question: How do the authors envision the dataset being used, and across which two dimensions of COVID-19 study?
questions.ground_truth: They hope the dataset can help the text mining community build downstream applications, and that it can bring insights for COVID-19 studies on both the biomedical side and the social side.
expected_passages: We hope this dataset can help the text mining community build downstream applications. We also hope this dataset can bring insights for the COVID-19 studies, both on the biomedical side and on the social side.
